OG_unit and the Simple, Improved and PMS protocols are boxed center/tabular pseudocode rather than algorithm environments; each box is one algorithm node with hand-segmented steps.

The prose descriptions of DOG (Sec. 4.2) and of the lazy renormalization scheme (Sec. 5.1) restate the pseudocode floats, so they got no algorithm node of their own; only the sentences that introduce symbols used later became definitions.

The proof of Corollary 5 says its high-probability bounds are proved 'as in the proof of Corollary 5' (its own label; Theorem 4 is probably meant). The finishing step skips this self-reference, and no edge was added for it.
One-sentence justifications next to Theorems 2, 3 and Corollary 6 were typed as prose proofs with proves edges, not as remarks. Theorem 2 also has its full appendix proof PP5.
lazyDOG, OD-DOG and PMS-with-reruns are defined in one sentence as compositions of earlier algorithms. They were typed as algorithms with no steps, since each is a single operation.
The Experiments section (data sets, figures), Related Work and Conclusions are not extracted. The only exceptions are two numerical claims about convergence and extra activations.

The total number of broadcasts is then |S|+2; using their calibrated clocks, each sensor (re)samples X_ensuremathv sim Poissonalpha p_ensuremathv and activates if X_ensuremathv ge 1. If no sensors activate before a specified timeout period, the default behavior is to rerun the sampling step. Eventually |S| ge 1 sensors activate in the same period. A distinguished sensor in S then determines the selected sensor ensuremathv, broadcasts ensuremathid(ensuremathv), and ensuremathv broadcasts its observed reward. selections in the variant of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace we describe 
(that uses the distributed multinomial sampling scheme and repeatedly reruns the protocol in

same as the original {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace.  Thus the regret bounds for

of sensors that activate in that round.  The total number of broadcasts is
then $|S|+2$; using their calibrated clocks, each sensor (re)samples

selects each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability
$(1-e^{-\alpha})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, because of the way the random bits
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ are shared in order to implement a coupled distribution for
sensor activation and selection.
Note that it would be sufficient to run the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace on the correct (possibly
oversampled) probabilities, $\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, 
since then~Prop.~\ref{thm:sampling} ensures that each $\ensuremath{v}$
is selected with probability $(1 - e^{-\alpha}) p_{\ensuremath{v}}$.
The difficulty is that $\ensuremath{v}$ does not have access to the correct
normalizer $Z(t)$, but only its estimate (lower bound) for it,
$Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
To overcome this difficulty, we define a joint probability
distribution over two random variables $(X_{\ensuremath{v}},
Y_{\ensuremath{v}})$, where 
\[
X_{\ensuremath{v}}  = X_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \left\{ 
\begin{array}{ll} 
1 & \text{if $R \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))$} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}  \right.
\]
\[
Y_{\ensuremath{v}} = Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \min \set{b \ :\ \sum_{a=0}^b \frac{e^{-\lambda}
    \lambda^{a}}{a!} \ge R }
\]
and $\lambda := \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$, and $R$ is
sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$.

\[
 e^{-\lambda}  \ge 1 - \lambda \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))
\]

Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)) \ge \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$ due to fact
that $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \le Z(t)$.

conservative indicator that $\ensuremath{v}$ should activate.

the sample from $\Poisson{\lambda}$ that $\ensuremath{v}$ would have
drawn had it known $Z(t)$.  The resulting distribution on selected
sensors is thus exactly the same as in the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace without lazy
renormalization.

the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} 
with $\epsilon = \gamma/\ensuremath{n}$ and $\hat{\epsilon} =
(e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}$.  Thus by Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} 
\begin{align*}
\E{\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} & \le \paren{1 +
  (e-1)/\alpha}\E{\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}\\ & = \paren{1 +
  (e-1)/\alpha} 
\end{align*}
because $\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) = 1$.
Each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ activates with probability $\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$,
so the expected number of activations is 
\[
\E{\alpha \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} \le \alpha\paren{1 +
  (e-1)/\alpha}\mbox{.}
\]

That proves the claimed bounds in expectation.  To prove bounds with
high probability, note that a sensor activates with probability
$\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ in round $t$, where   $q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ is a
random variable.
Fix $t$.  Let $[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}]$ denote the indicator variable
for the event $\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}$, i.e., $[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}] = 1$ if $\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}$ occurs, and
$[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}] = 0$ otherwise.  Then we can write 
$[\ensuremath{v} \text{ activates in round }t] = [\alpha
q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge R]$, where $R$ is sampled uniformly at random from
$[0,1]$ and $R$ is independent of $q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
Then if $f_R$ is the probability density functions of $R$ we can write 
\[
\begin{aligned}
   \prob{R \le \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha
q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge R \ |\  R = r} f_R(r) dr\\
  & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge r} f_R(r) dr \\
& = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge r}dr \\
& = \E{ \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) }
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the number of sensor activations is a sum of $|V|$ binary
random variables with cumulative mean 
$\mu := \sum_{\ensuremath{v}}  \E{ \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) }$.
We have already bounded this mean as $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$.
From here a simple application of a Chernoff-Hoeffding bound suffices
to prove that with high probability this sum is at most 
$\mathcal{O}(\alpha + \log n)$.  Let $A$ be the number of sensor activations.
Then, e.g., Theorem~$5$ of~\cite{CL06} 
immediately implies 
\[
\prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ - \frac{\delta^2
    \mu^2}{2 \mu + \frac{2\delta \mu}{3}}}
\]
For $\delta \ge 1$, this yields 
$\prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ -
  \frac{3\delta\mu}{8}}$.
Setting $\delta = 1 + \frac{8c\ln n}{3\mu}$ ensures this probability is
at most $n^{-c}$, hence 
$\prob{A \ge 2\mu + \frac{8}{3}c\ln n} \le n^{-c}$.
Noting that $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$ completes the high probability
bound on the number of activations.


As for the number of messages, note that each message involves a
sensor as sender or receiver, and by inspection the protocol only
involves two messages per activated node.
